Here's where things stand — good progress on all three fronts from the handoff:

**1. `internal-hook` dispatcher — built, tested, committed, and verified live** (commit `6683627`). This was the gap where real commits got no identity. The new hidden CLI command dispatches the three git hooks: `commit-msg` injects the `Change-Id` trailer via `git interpret-trailers` (verified it lands before comment blocks and `commit -v` scissors sections, with guards for already-present Gerrit trailers and empty messages), `post-commit` records the commit into the change-map, and `post-rewrite` folds rewrites from stdin pairs. Like capture-session, it always exits 0 so a hook can never break a commit, logging failures to `.git-for-ai/hooks.log`. The proof is the commit itself: it went through the repo's own hooks and came out with trailer `Ifacade3f…`, a change-map entry showing `origin: post-commit / trailer: seen` (no more orphan-recovery), and a captured session linked in the ledger — the full pipeline working on a real commit for the first time.

**2. The M9 sqlite blocker is resolved.** Node's built-in `node:sqlite` on Node 24.8 loads the prebuilt `sqlite-vec` extension cleanly — I verified `vec0` KNN queries and FTS5 both work in the same database. No native compilation needed at all, so `better-sqlite3` stays gone and no VS/ClangCL fixing was required.

**3. M9 (embeddings, chunking, vector store) is now running** as a background Fable agent, briefed per the established pattern — doc sections cited, hard scope boundary (core embeddings only, no CLI), real-fixture tests required, and the sqlite decision baked in as non-negotiable. I'll review its output, independently re-run the build and tests, and commit when it lands.

Also fixed in passing: two CLI test files were flaking under parallel `turbo test` because they never got the 60-second timeout the other git-heavy suites set per-file — that's now a package-level vitest config for both `cli` and `core`. Full suite is green: 276 tests (156 core, 59 CLI including 12 new, 61 schemas).

Good timing — M9 is running in the background, so this is a natural stopping point for review. Let me gather the visible output first, then ground the discussion in what the architecture docs promised versus your vision.

M9 is chugging along in the background, so this is a good moment. Here's the review — including one real problem I found in yesterday's build by inspecting the live data, and one gap that matters a lot for your vision specifically.

## What's actually visible today, on this repo

`git for-ai log --intent` — every commit annotated with its change-id, the agent-captured intent summary, and provenance:

```
6683627  facade3f  Implement internal-hook dispatcher: real commits now get identity  [agent]
7d4cd73  1b4aba46  Add session handoff doc; mark M1-M8 done in CLI_PLAN.md           [agent]
8e25afb  1b4aba46  M7: implement session capture - the differentiator                [agent]
5ce284f  702a2df1  First working CLI: init + log --intent, wired end-to-end          [agent, conf 0.88]
8b27d08  6146d58c  Implement the change-id resolver: identity that survives…         [agent, conf 0.85]
73bda1f  —         M4: implement @git-for-ai/core ledger read/write                  [no intent: pre-git-for-ai]
```

`git for-ai show <commit>` — the full enhanced record behind one commit. For this morning's commit it shows: the change identity (`facade3f…`, `origin: post-commit, trailer: seen` — assigned properly by the new hooks), the ledger entry (summary, the exact files in scope, which agent/model made it), and the linked session capture — this very conversation's tool calls, redacted and content-addressed into `refs/git-for-ai/sessions`. With `--session` you get the span-by-span trace: which commands the agent ran, what it edited, timestamped. The M7 session from yesterday holds 348 real spans; this morning's holds the actual `interpret-trailers` experiments that shaped the dispatcher design.

All of it lives in git refs — it pushes/fetches like any ref, no sidecar database. And `--json` exists on `log`/`show`, so an agent can already consume everything machine-readably. The testbed repo (`git-for-ai-testbed`) shows the same layering over a vanilla web app's history.

## Reviewing against your vision, two things need revisiting

**1. A real bug from yesterday, caught live just now: the R4 "inferred continuation" branch is misattributing commits.** Look at the log above — the M7 commit and the handoff-doc commit share change-id `1b4aba46`. They're unrelated changes, but yesterday (pre-dispatcher) commits had no trailers, so the resolver fell to R4: "single parent with known change-id + tree similarity over 70% → same logical change." The flaw: whole-tree similarity is the wrong signal, because *any small commit* leaves >70% of the tree identical to its parent. In a repo of real size R4 will fire for nearly every trailerless commit, gluing distinct changes together. The visible damage: the handoff-doc's ledger entry now *supersedes* the M7 entry, so `show 8e25afb` presents the wrong effective summary and buries the 348-span M7 session as "superseded." Going forward the new commit-msg hook makes R4 nearly moot for fresh commits — but R4 is exactly what runs when someone adopts git-for-ai on an *existing* repo, which is the most common onboarding path. I'd fix it by requiring diff-overlap (the changed paths resemble the change's previous diff), not tree-overlap — or dropping R4 to "never infer, let `doctor` flag and `relink` decide." Small fix in `resolve.ts`, plus a `relink` of the two miswired commits here.

**2. The bigger strategic gap: there is no way for an agent to deliberately *say* anything.** This is the one that cuts against your vision most directly. The data model already defines exactly what you're describing — the ledger's `reasoning` block has `intent`, `constraints`, `rejected` (alternatives + why rejected), `confidence`, `scope_risk`, `reversibility`, `tested`, `related`. But today the *only* writer is passive session capture, and it populates just `reasoning.intent` (first line of a captured plan). Nothing exposes the rest. An agent that just spent 20 minutes discovering "Redis was rejected because we can't add infra" has no command to record that — the schema is rich, the write path is a sliver of it. There's no `annotate`-style command anywhere in CLI_REFERENCE either; this is a genuine hole in the original design relative to what you want, not just an unbuilt milestone. The fix is cheap because `appendLedgerEntry` already exists: a `git for-ai annotate` command taking structured JSON on stdin (agent-friendly) or flags (human-friendly), appending a full-reasoning ledger entry to HEAD or any commit/change. I'd also have `capture-session` mine more of the transcript into `reasoning` (e.g., `tested` from the test commands it already sees in spans).

## What I'd build next, in order

1. **`git for-ai annotate`** — the explicit agent write path. Highest vision-alignment per unit effort, unblocked, small.
2. **Fix R4 + relink the two miswired commits** — data quality underpins everything else; also small.
3. **M10 `reindex` → M11/M12 `ask` / `blame --why`** once M9 lands — this is the read side for agents: "why is this line like this?" answered from ledger + sessions + code semantically. This was always the plan and it serves the vision directly.
4. Then a decision point later: **M13 `sync` vs. an MCP server** (`packages/server` placeholder exists). If the primary consumer is an agent, exposing `ask`/`show`/`annotate` as MCP tools may be worth doing *before* multi-machine sync — a Claude Code instance in any repo could then query and write intent natively. That reordering is yours to call when we get there.

One honest note on scope: items 1 and 2 touch `core` outside the M9 agent's sandbox (it's confined to `embeddings/`), so I can start them without conflict whenever you give the word. What's your take — agree with annotate-first, and any reactions on the R4 fix approach (diff-overlap vs. kill-R4-and-relink-manually) or the MCP-before-sync question?
Let me review the wider-system plans first — the monorepo plan and the placeholder package READMEs — then I'll lay out both plans.
